Geopolitics & Diplomacy
• BRICS leaders convened in New Delhi, with Modi hosting Xi and Putin as tariffs, wars and proposals to link domestic payment systems cross-border dominated the agenda.
• Donald Trump began a two-day visit to Ireland, meeting leaders in Dublin and touting ties “stronger than ever” before attending the Irish Open in Doonbeg.
• Sweden votes Sunday in a knife-edge election focused on migration, crime and the economy, with polls suggesting the far right could enter government for the first time.
• Newly declassified CIA documents show U.S. presidents received warnings about Osama bin Laden and al-Qaeda prior to the 9/11 attacks.
Why it matters: These developments reflect shifting power blocs, electoral volatility in Europe, and ongoing reassessments of U.S. security and alliances.

Society & Human Rights
• Kenya’s crackdown on foreign traders has sparked fear and flight among migrants as authorities struggle to contain the fallout.
• On the 25th anniversary of 9/11, analysts argue the “War on Terror” helped mainstream far-right Islamophobia in Europe.
• In Gaza and the Palestinian cultural sphere, weddings and archival preservation have become acts of defiance and continuity amid war and occupation.
• London councils have seized more than 3,000 hazardously parked e-bikes this year, highlighting tensions over public space and regulation.
Why it matters: Social cohesion, civil liberties and the governance of public spaces remain under strain across regions facing conflict, migration and polarization.

Armed Conflict & Security
• Saudi Arabia shut a key East–West oil pipeline after a drone attack launched from Iraq; the U.S. also limited air-defense support windows for tankers transiting Hormuz.
• Yemen’s Houthi rebels captured a strategic Red Sea island as fighting re-erupted, heightening risks to shipping and Saudi exports.
• Russia said it struck cargo vessels and steel plants across Ukraine; Afghans continue to reckon with the legacy of the U.S.-led war nearly 25 years on.
• A ferry fire off the Philippines has killed at least 35 people, with officials warning the toll could rise as recovery continues.
Why it matters: Energy infrastructure, maritime routes and civilian safety are increasingly exposed amid overlapping conflicts and security gaps.

• U.S. wildfire crews have used glutathione to ease smoke exposure, but unions warn the antioxidant treatment may pose risks and lacks clear oversight.
• Documents suggest hundreds of London Underground workers may have been exposed to asbestos without properly fitted masks over two decades.
• A hypervirulent MRSA strain linked to a bouncy castle infected 48 children in Ireland, underscoring outbreak risks in communal environments.
Why it matters: Worker safety and infectious disease control remain critical as authorities balance novel interventions with established protections.

Art & Culture
• European galleries report increasingly brazen thefts, with art crime experts warning of faster, riskier museum burglaries.
• A West Sussex exhibition reframes rewilding sites as visually compelling, celebrating deadwood, scrub and beaver-felled trees.
• Nashville International Airport is set to be renamed in honor of Dolly Parton after a unanimous board vote.
Why it matters: Cultural institutions and landscapes are both being reinterpreted—and challenged—by security trends and evolving public values.

Economy & Markets
• Oil prices face further upward pressure after Saudi Arabia shut the East–West pipeline used to bypass Hormuz, following drone attacks.
• Oracle posted strong AI cloud-driven revenue growth but faces scrutiny over debt; founder Larry Ellison adopted a plan to sell up to $7.5 billion in stock.
• More than 120 organizations urged removal of levies amounting to about 10% of UK energy bills; UK data show AI is denting job prospects for computer science graduates.
• India’s SEBI proposed changes to a contentious closing auction mechanism amid liquidity concerns, while catastrophe bonds could expand to cover data center risks.
Why it matters: Energy shocks, AI-driven market shifts, and regulatory recalibrations are reshaping corporate strategies, labor prospects and investor risk.

Artificial Intelligence
• Safety concerns intensified after an Anthropic researcher warned of a race toward self-improving AI; lawmakers called for regulation as investors debated “doomer” narratives and Trump dismissed extinction risks.
• Courts and platforms confronted AI misuse: a lawyer was fined for citing fabricated AI testimony; users bypassed Claude’s bioweapons safeguards; Meta adjusted AI prompts and faces a class-action over training data and face recognition.
• New deployments spotlight capability gains: OpenAI’s GPT‑6 Astra is improving software testing and operations, NASA and IBM launched a lunar AI model, and AI helped reveal hidden human proteins.
• Industry momentum continues with Moonshot AI targeting $2B in annual revenue and researchers proposing chiplet and memory-controller advances to accelerate and secure LLM inference.
Why it matters: The pace of AI innovation is colliding with safety, legal and governance challenges, even as real-world applications proliferate.

Science & Technology
• Consumer tech churns ahead with apparent leaks of Meta’s slim “Project Phoenix” headset, AirPods 5 preorders adding ANC, and Ikea’s budget Badkruka speaker with optical input.
• Rocket Lab launched a mystery Earth-observation satellite for a secret customer, as NASA invites citizen scientists to help vet space telescope data and explores a U.S. Space Academy.
• Research highlights include proteomic insights into ancient Egyptian materials, advances linking interfacial water structure to photocatalytic hydrogen evolution, and an RNA “nucleotide flip” that activates fluorescent dyes.
• New astronomy findings suggest the sun may have swallowed a super‑Earth in its early history, while a nearby Type Ia supernova offers a rare observing opportunity for amateurs.
Why it matters: Hardware releases, space initiatives and cross‑disciplinary science continue to broaden access to technology and deepen understanding of our world and beyond.

Climate & Environment
• A U.S. court threw out the government’s “energy emergency” used to extend coal plant operations, as communities scrutinize fossil‑fuel exceptions.
• Data centers’ environmental footprint drew ire: Oracle pledged to match Stargate emissions with renewables, while an analysis tied SpaceXAI’s Mississippi facility to a nitrogen oxide spike.
• Water scarcity threatens industrial growth, with Arizona set to lose over a quarter of its Colorado River allotment, complicating semiconductor plans; Indonesia’s El Niño‑driven fires are on track for century‑high emissions.
• Policy signals are mixed: the UK delayed a North Sea gasfield decision ahead of a byelection; Santa Monica canceled a beach festival due to storm‑driven erosion.
Why it matters: Climate stressors are constraining infrastructure, industry and events, forcing hard choices on energy, regulation and resilience.

Why it matters: Understanding immune‑brain interactions and testing therapies that shift biological aging markers could shape future treatments for neurodegeneration and age‑related disease.

Society & Human Rights.text: For this year’s IEEE annual election, the IEEE Tellers Committee will recognize the Sections with the highest voter turnout (based on total eligible voters) in each Region with an incentive reward after the election results are accepted by the IEEE Board of Directors.The incentive initiative is managed by the Tellers Committee, which retains full authority over all rules, operations, and decisions regarding the program.Incentive guidelines The Section sizes and their respective reward amounts are:Large sections consist of more than 1,501 eligible voting members. The top-performing large section in each IEEE region will be rewarded with US $1,000.Medium sections consist of 501 to 1,500 eligible voting members. Each region’s top-performing medium section will receive $600.Small sections consist of 500 or fewer eligible voting members. The top-performing small section in each region will receive $400.To learn more about the incentive program, visit the IEEE annual election website. If you haven’t voted in the 2026 elections, you can learn about the candidates and vote here. Send questions to: elections@ieee.org.

Art & Culture.title: Take a Look Inside Ome Dezin’s 4,500-Square-Foot Hollywood Hills Restoration
Art & Culture.text: SummaryOme Dezin restored a 4,500-square-foot Hollywood Hills home originally designed by Jeffrey Mills.Interiors feature natural stone, warm woods and a custom stained-glass kitchen pantry.A mirrored exterior sauna houses a vibrant kiwi glass and granite bathroom.Los Angeles-based design firm Ome Dezin has unveiled its latest residential project, a stunning 4,500-square-foot property nestled behind a gated drive on over an acre in the Hollywood Hills, Los Angeles. Originally built in 1997 by architect Jeffrey Mills, the contemporary home was initially conceived with a strong emphasis on natural light and a seamless connection to the outdoors. Over the decades, the residence has boasted a rich history, previously serving as an art gallery and the private residence of an A-list Hollywood actor. In its meticulous restoration, Ome Dezin preserved the property's unique architectural history while thoroughly reimagining its aesthetic footprint.Drawing direct cues from the original architecture and the surrounding woodland landscape, Ome Dezin altered 99% of the home's interior surfaces to further soften the boundary between indoors and out. The refined material palette relies on warm woods, richly veined natural stone, sleek stainless steel, and expansive glass, creating a serene environment that feels deeply connected to its natural setting. A standout feature of the interior is a custom kitchen pantry framed by stained-glass doors; a hidden window positioned behind the glass casts beautiful highlights of color and natural light into the kitchen and hallway, bringing an artful warmth to the space.The property’s most striking addition is a newly constructed, mirrored structure designed to house a sauna and full bathroom. Inspired by Doug Aitken’s Mirage - a famous mirror-clad home installation in the desert - the detached building essentially disappears into the forest, reflecting the landscape rather than interrupting it. A distinctive circular cutout acts as an architectural portal framing views toward the pool. In sharp contrast to its quiet, camouflaged exterior, the structure's interior delivers a vibrant, otherworldly mood. The bathroom is enveloped entirely in two materials: kiwi-colored glass by Zia Tile and Palladium Arte Granite stone. This saturated palette draws directly from the vivid hues of brightly colored tree frogs, creating an immersive, nature-inspired experience.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Art & Culture.title: Welcome to Maurizio Cattelan’s “Church” of Failure
Art & Culture.text: SummaryItalian artist Maurizio Cattelan opens a new solo exhibition, 'Night,' at the Neue Nationalgalerie in BerlinOn through March 7, 2027, the exhibition is imagined as a "contemporary church" and features hyperrealistic sculptures exploring authority, religion, and mortalityA fire extinguisher might be the easiest piece in Maurizio Cattelan's new Berlin show to miss. But "Dust," perched at the entrance of Ludwig Mies van der Rohe’s modernist glass hall, is also the most significant. Inside are the ashes of the artist's friend.This is just the first piece of Night, now on view at Neue Nationalgalerie. For decades, Cattelan has held down quite the reputation as conceptual art's enfant terrible. His often provocative work unsettles our relationship to authority, value, and mortality, revealing humanity's weaknesses in the process. In his first major go-around at a German museum, the Italian artist skips the tongue-in-cheek pieces he's best known for — like the taped banana or solid-gold toilet, dubbed "America" — instead, bringing new commissions and works from the past 30 years that bend towards the sinister.To enter, visitors must pass through "Purgatory," a scaled-down Brandenburg Gate, confronting ambiguity and division that shapes the historic no-man's land. At the center, "Him" — Cattelan’s infamous miniaturized Hitler, kneeling in prayer — faces "Dawn," a crucified woman suspended in a transport crate.On the rafts above, in "People," thousands of taxidermied pigeons glare down on passersby below. Other animals nearby explore themes of exhaustion and labor: a dead horse hangs midair in "Novecento," while "Pentecost" similarly sees a donkey up high, struggling under the weight of an overloaded cart."Night is not simply the absence of light. It is a condition. The exhibition is not about darkness. It is about the loss of certainty," Cattelan wrote in a press release. "And while failure and despair seem to prevail for now, salvation, reflection, and imagination await on the other side. The space, after all, was imagined "like a contemporary church," fitting to both the architecture and the artist's own fraught relationship with Catholicism. "Night is also temporary," he continued, "it always contains the possibility of morning, even if you cannot see it yet."The exhibition is now on view in Berlin until March 7, 2027.Neue NationalgaleriePotsdamer Str. 50,10785 Berlin,GermanyClick here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.text: SummaryHouse of Errors has built its most detailed capsule yet around paint splatters rendered entirely in embroideryThe lead jacket carries 1,500,000 individual stitches while the matching carpenter jeans hold 1,150,000A hoodie, two caps, two knitted rugbys and a tee complete the eight-piece lineupHouse of Errors has released The Paint Collection, a Fall/Winter 2026 capsule in which every paint splatter is stitched rather than printed or dyed. The London label has scaled up a concept it first tested on a single hero piece from its 6 Year Anniversary collection, expanding it into a full run of garments where the artwork exists as thread.The Embroidered Paint Workwear Jacket sets the benchmark at 1,500,000 individual stitches. Beyond the embroidery, it runs a brown corduroy collar, a YKK zip and bespoke hardware developed for the capsule. The Embroidered Carpenter Jeans follow with 1,150,000 threads and the same custom hardware, putting both halves of the set above a million stitches apiece.The detail work does not stop at the splatter itself.
